title: Itachi vs Obito, Kakashi, Minato and Madara: Who Wins Each Fight?
description: Itachi vs Obito, Kakashi, Minato and Madara: four Naruto matchups explained through canon encounters, Kamui, Tsukuyomi, Flying Raijin, Susanoo and character versions.
keywords: Itachi vs Obito, Itachi vs Kakashi, Itachi vs Minato, Itachi vs Madara, Naruto Itachi matchups, Itachi versus Madara, DMS Kakashi vs Itachi, Minato Flying Raijin versus Itachi, Tsukuyomi vs Kamui
summary: Early Itachi decisively incapacitates Kakashi with Tsukuyomi in their canon encounter. Itachi has no definitive canonical one-on-one duel against Obito, Minato or Madara. In specific hypothetical versions, we lean masked Obito for Kamui, living Minato for Flying Raijin's positional control, and war-era Madara for overwhelming scale. Later Kakashi forms must be compared separately from the Kakashi Itachi actually faced.

sections: Four Itachi matchups, but not four canon fights

What makes Itachi-versus debates so enduring is that his greatest weapon is rarely the most visible one. He can end a confrontation before his opponent understands what was real. Put that approach against Obito's intangibility, Kakashi's evolving Sharingan, Minato's teleportation or Madara's overwhelming battlefield power, and there is no single rule that settles every encounter. Saying Itachi wins because he is a genius explains too little. So does saying he loses because the other character looks faster or has a larger Susanoo.

There is a crucial factual distinction at the beginning. Itachi and Kakashi actually confront one another, and their early encounter ends with Kakashi incapacitated by Tsukuyomi. The series does not provide equivalent completed, decisive one-on-one battles between Itachi and Obito, Minato or Madara. Those three are hypothetical comparisons based on demonstrated techniques. This guide separates what the manga and anime show from what we can reasonably infer. Major Naruto Shippuden spoilers follow, including revelations about the Uchiha, reanimation and the Fourth Great Ninja War.
The answer in brief: our conditional verdicts

Against the masked Obito, we lean toward Obito in an unprepared fight. Kamui gives him an unusual ability to deny physical contact, making Itachi's strongest finishing options difficult to deliver. Itachi's tactical intelligence and genjutsu leave room for an upset if he understands the technique and prepares a specific trap. Against early-series Kakashi, there is no need to speculate about the recorded encounter: Itachi's Tsukuyomi wins the exchange. Later war Kakashi is a different question, and the brief double-Mangekyo version from the Kaguya fight is different again.

Against living Fourth Hokage Minato, our judgment leans toward Minato because Flying Raijin can control position and timing while Itachi's ill body cannot sustain an endless exchange. Itachi still has real routes through a carefully applied illusion or sealing strike. Against reanimated war-era Madara, the evidence strongly favors Madara, whose clones, battlefield-scale attacks and Perfect Susanoo surpass Itachi's demonstrated output. The Ten-Tails version creates an even wider mismatch. These are editorial assessments, not odds calculated by the creator or official rankings issued by the franchise.
Before comparing anyone, specify the character version

Naruto has an unusual habit of changing the terms of a matchup late in the story. The Itachi who fights Sasuke is seriously ill and physically deteriorating; the Itachi brought back through Edo Tensei no longer faces those limits in the same way. Kakashi first faces Itachi long before he learns to use Kamui as effectively as he does during the war. His final temporary double-Mangekyo power is not something he can draw on throughout his career. A fair analysis cannot grant him those abilities in his earlier encounter and claim to be describing canon.

The same warning applies to Obito and Madara. Masked Obito's use of Kamui is not equivalent to the Ten-Tails jinchuriki's capabilities. Reanimated Madara's performance against the Five Kage is not a mere preview of a conventional young Uchiha with the same health and equipment as Itachi. Minato also has an ordinary living form and a later reanimated form with access to Kurama's chakra. When a fan discussion combines every person's best moment without declaring these changes, it creates an imaginary character on each side. That is a fun game, perhaps, but it should not be mistaken for evidence.
Itachi's toolkit: more than a list of powerful eye techniques

Itachi's advantage begins with information. His Sharingan lets him read and anticipate movements, while his genjutsu can make an opponent waste a critical moment responding to something that did not happen. Tsukuyomi punishes particular visual engagement with intense mental suffering. Amaterasu brings dangerous black flames into the fight. Susanoo adds protection, and its Totsuka Blade gives him a sealing option. The Yata Mirror is associated with that defensive arsenal. These abilities work differently, but they share a theme: Itachi wants to create a moment when the opponent's safest-looking choice is actually the mistake.

His strengths come with conditions. Illness limits the living Itachi of the later story, and using powerful Mangekyo techniques is physically demanding. Izanami requires a particular setup and sacrifices sight in the eye used; the war-arc fight with Kabuto is not proof that it can defeat any person on demand. Kotoamatsukami originated with Shisui's preserved eye and a carefully arranged crow contingency, rather than being a native attack that Itachi can cast freely every few seconds. Give Itachi his real abilities and he remains dangerous enough. He does not need powers the story never shows him possessing.
Itachi vs Obito: Kamui changes the meaning of an attack

A conventional fighter can usually be threatened by a sufficiently fast or well-timed strike. Obito makes that assumption unreliable. His Kamui can shift relevant parts of his body through a connected time-space dimension, letting attacks appear to pass through him. The official Naruto war retrospective describes the alliance struggling with this defense until Kakashi recognizes how his own Kamui interacts with it. Their coordinated attacks then reveal a genuine opening. This proves Obito's technique is formidable, not that his body exists beyond all possible harm.

For Itachi, the challenge is to create the moment Obito has to become tangible. An Amaterasu cast, a shuriken feint or a Susanoo attack may all demand a response, but merely launching the technique is not enough. Itachi would have to anticipate where the target will be, what action forces physical interaction and whether an evasion route is still available. That is an interesting tactical puzzle for a precise fighter. Obito, meanwhile, can choose to withdraw and make a sick opponent spend resources trying to create an opening that may never appear. Those asymmetrical demands are why we lean Obito in a first encounter.
Itachi vs Obito: could Tsukuyomi beat him?

A common argument says Itachi only needs to meet Obito's eyes. This skips the most difficult question: does that valid encounter occur under conditions where the illusion is successfully applied? Obito has extensive Sharingan experience and uses deception as an everyday tool. That does not make him officially immune to Tsukuyomi. But Itachi has never demonstrated a successful Tsukuyomi against Obito in a completed canon duel either. Both universal claims would go further than the source material allows.

One scenario favors Itachi more than a random brawl: he knows the opponent's technique and engineers an apparent safe opportunity for Obito to look or move in the wrong way. Another favors Obito: he has advance knowledge of Itachi's genjutsu, refuses predictable visual engagement and makes his opponent chase a body that repeatedly vanishes. This is a contest about information as much as chakra. The fact that both fighters are intelligent Uchiha does not settle whose deception works first. We can identify the risk without inventing a definitive unseen exchange.
Itachi vs Obito: Amaterasu and the Totsuka Blade

Amaterasu would be dangerous if its flames reached Obito at a vulnerable instant, and using the fire to constrain space might help Itachi read an evasion pattern. The black flames are not, however, documented as a universal switch that permanently disables Kamui. The same care is needed when discussing the Totsuka Blade. Its sealing effect could be devastating if delivered, but a lethal effect is not evidence that contact is guaranteed. Obito's very best defensive quality is denying that contact.

Itachi's Susanoo might protect him from a sudden approach, but making his own position obvious can also help an opponent who can disengage. Obito must become vulnerable at certain moments to perform particular physical actions; Itachi might exploit one of them. Yet knowing that a window exists and successfully hitting it are different achievements. The narrative never stages a clean contest between these weapons and Obito's complete kit. Our verdict therefore recognizes a plausible Itachi ambush or trap without assuming he executes it whenever asked.
Itachi vs Obito: the version-dependent verdict

For living, late-life Itachi versus masked Obito, both entering without preparation, Obito has the clearer route to controlling the pace. He can make Itachi prove that an attack will connect while he looks for the moment to capture or punish the opponent. This does not mean Obito would defeat Itachi instantly or that every interaction would favor him. It means the defensive problem he presents is particularly difficult for someone who has limited time and must commit to costly techniques.

If Itachi knows exactly how Kamui's dimensional interaction works and has enough time to arrange the battlefield, his prospects improve. If instead the comparison uses Ten-Tails Obito, the argument changes dramatically: the official war narrative documents power, endurance and defenses beyond the masked man's ordinary state. In that later matchup, we would strongly favor Obito. Anyone giving a single final percentage for every incarnation of both characters is hiding the very assumptions that determine the outcome.
Itachi vs Kakashi: this fight really happened

The original Naruto story includes the decisive evidence. Itachi and Kisame appear in the Leaf and face shinobi including Asuma, Kurenai and Kakashi. Kakashi joins the confrontation, only to suffer Itachi's Mangekyo technique Tsukuyomi. The official Naruto twentieth-anniversary retrospective describes the attack and Kakashi's mental ordeal. The original anime directory identifies their encounter in episode 82, Eye to Eye, Sharingan vs. Sharingan. The confirmed result is that Itachi overwhelms Kakashi in that critical genjutsu exchange.

This encounter makes a specific point about the Sharingan. Possessing an eye of the same family is not automatic immunity from an advanced visual technique. Kakashi is exceptionally skilled, yet he cannot safely handle what Itachi subjects him to in that moment. At the same time, this is not a contest between every form the two shinobi will ever possess. Kakashi continues growing through Shippuden, and later powers change the methods available to him. We should respect the actual result without extending it into a rule that future Kakashi must always lose the same way.
Itachi vs Kakashi: does war-era Kamui change the answer?

War-era Kakashi has a more developed spatial option. During the confrontation with Obito, he helps identify that the two Kamui abilities lead to the same dimension, then contributes to a coordinated counter. The official war summary shows the team turning a seemingly untouchable opponent into one they can hit. That feat combines observation, spatial technique and timing. It would give late Kakashi an entirely different way to threaten Itachi compared with their first encounter, which turned on visual genjutsu.

There is an important limitation: Kamui is taxing. The same official recap notes Kakashi exhausting substantial chakra through repeated use and needing help to continue. A late-war Itachi versus Kakashi fight might therefore come down to which one secures a decisive application before paying an unsustainable cost. Can Kakashi get an accurate Kamui attack without offering a Tsukuyomi opportunity? Can Itachi impose a convincing illusion before Kakashi attacks through the spatial route? Those are useful hypothetical questions, but neither has an official on-screen answer.
Itachi vs Kakashi: what about DMS Kakashi?

Near the finale, Kakashi receives a brief, extraordinary gift connected to Obito's Mangekyo powers and fights beside Team 7 against Kaguya. The official Naruto finale recap documents his use of Susanoo and Kamui-enhanced techniques. Fans call this temporary state DMS Kakashi. It is important to remember that he does not maintain those powers as his normal permanent equipment. Using them to rewrite what happened during his first meeting with Itachi would be a mistake about the timeline.

If the comparison explicitly allows temporary double-Mangekyo Kakashi against living Itachi, we favor Kakashi. The available offensive and defensive options have changed too drastically to treat this as a replay of the early Tsukuyomi encounter. This is a hypothetical judgment, not a canon rematch. The defensible three-part summary is straightforward: early Kakashi lost the real genjutsu encounter; ordinary war Kakashi presents a more complicated hypothetical; the exceptionally empowered temporary DMS version has the stronger hypothetical position.
Why Itachi and Kakashi are such interesting opponents

Both are patient observers, but they use information differently. Kakashi reads the situation, learns from others and coordinates unconventional solutions. Itachi prefers to control what the opponent believes before the fight's decisive move. Their early exchange demonstrates the cost of letting Itachi establish that control. Their hypothetical later meeting would ask whether Kakashi could reverse the information advantage using his knowledge of ocular techniques, battlefield positioning and Kamui.

A comparison framed solely as whose Sharingan is stronger misses the emotional shape of Naruto's writing. Kakashi becomes a teacher partly because he knows the cost of loss and secrecy. Itachi repeatedly keeps the truth from the people closest to him. The two embody very different ways of handling painful knowledge. That does not decide a fight, but it offers readers a more distinctive reason to revisit their scenes than a recycled ranking of jutsu names.
Itachi vs Minato: why the opening second matters

Itachi and the Fourth Hokage do not have a canon one-on-one duel settling their superiority. Their abilities nevertheless make a compelling hypothetical. Minato's Flying Raijin teleports him to marked points, allowing him to change position without running across the intervening space. The Naruto official database explains how the marks work and distinguishes Minato's virtually unrestricted use of the technique from limitations placed on a later adaptation. Movement, positioning and immediate attack timing are major parts of his combat identity.

Itachi would normally try to shape an opponent's perception of range, line of sight and the next attack. Minato can abandon a location almost instantaneously, which complicates those expectations. Yet teleportation is not clairvoyance. Minato must choose where to place markers and when to act, and he can still make wrong assessments. A smart Itachi might exploit the expectation that a particular marker is safe. A smart Minato might refuse to let Itachi establish the eye-contact or sealing window in the first place.
Itachi vs Minato: the masked-man encounter is relevant, not decisive

During the Nine-Tails attack, Minato confronts the masked man and finds a way to strike at the correct moment despite the opponent's space-time technique. The official Naruto retrospective describes him breaking the masked figure's control and forcing a retreat. That is excellent evidence for Minato's ability to identify a vulnerability quickly, not evidence that he has already defeated Itachi. Obito's technique and Itachi's techniques are different problems.

This distinction protects the argument from an easy but false syllogism. Minato counters the masked man, therefore he must be immune to Tsukuyomi: that conclusion does not follow. The scene instead shows why Minato is a strong tactical candidate. He can read a dangerous encounter, time a teleportation and seize the instant in which an attack is possible. Itachi has similar strengths in deception and anticipation. A hypothetical clash would be a contest over whose interpretation of the opening is right.
Itachi vs Minato: can teleportation escape genjutsu?

Speed does not automatically prevent a mental attack once its relevant conditions have been met. Itachi's Tsukuyomi is not a conventional projectile that Minato simply outruns. Equally, merely possessing the technique does not establish that Itachi will land it against someone who can change positions abruptly and understands the importance of dangerous eye contact. The story does not provide a laboratory-style test of Minato against Itachi's Mangekyo, so confident claims of instant success or perfect immunity are speculative.

For a useful comparison, imagine both fighters with no advance information. Minato probes the distance while Itachi tries to identify the pattern behind sudden movement. Now give both knowledge. Minato becomes more cautious about visual engagement; Itachi may look for a predictable marker or apparent escape route to exploit. Neither scenario changes their fundamental techniques, but it changes their likely behavior. That is why intelligence and preparation should be stated rather than silently granted to whichever character a writer wants to win.
Itachi vs Minato: Rasengan, Susanoo and stamina

Minato can deliver Rasengan after a well-chosen teleport, forcing the defender to respond with remarkable speed. Itachi might use an illusion or Susanoo, especially if he knows an attack is coming. But activating an impressive defense does not automatically let him hold a teleporting opponent in place. Minato can withdraw, reposition and search for another angle. Amaterasu might make parts of the arena dangerous, yet Flying Raijin can reduce dependence on an ordinary route through the fire.

The duration of the fight is important. Living Itachi's health is explicitly compromised by the time he faces Sasuke. A long contest with repeated high-cost Mangekyo techniques works against him. Minato still has to expend attention and chakra, but his ability to choose when the fighters come into direct contact gives him a structural advantage in a standard encounter. Itachi's best hope may be to make a particular moment look safe and end the fight there. This is why we favor Minato without denying that a well-timed Itachi trap could succeed.
Itachi vs Minato: our conditional verdict

For living Fourth Hokage Minato versus living, illness-affected Itachi, we lean Minato because Flying Raijin repeatedly challenges Itachi's control of spacing and timing. Minato's response to the masked man supports that assessment with a demonstrated example. That is not a claim of absolute genjutsu immunity or that Minato would never lose a tactical exchange. It is a judgment about which character can more consistently enforce the sort of fight he wants.

If Itachi is reanimated, ordinary stamina and injury assumptions change. If Minato is given his later reanimated Kurama-enhanced abilities, the comparison shifts in another direction. If either fighter has arranged the battlefield in advance, markers and traps become more important than raw speed rhetoric. We would not describe those cases as the same fight. A verdict is useful only when a reader can see the conditions that produced it.
Itachi vs Madara: the largest difference in demonstrated power

Madara is the clearest unfavorable matchup for Itachi once we use his demonstrated war-era form. The official Naruto Madara retrospective shows him fighting large Allied Shinobi Forces formations with powerful fire style, Susanoo, Rinnegan and destructive meteorites. In the Five Kage confrontation, he uses twenty-five wood clones capable of employing Susanoo, then manifests the tremendous Perfect Susanoo. These are actual story events, not numbers fabricated by a fan power chart.

Itachi is an exceptionally dangerous single-combat tactician, but being able to outthink one opponent does not answer multiple capable clones and large-scale assaults at the same time. Both men are Uchiha and both possess Susanoo, yet those shared labels do not mean their shown output is equal. Madara can impose a level of battlefield pressure that makes Itachi's careful attempts to arrange one decisive opening far more difficult. A good analysis should acknowledge that difference before raising unusual possible counters.
Itachi vs Madara: would Tsukuyomi be enough?

Tsukuyomi is still a serious threat, and readers are justified in asking whether Madara could be caught by an extraordinary visual illusion. The manga, however, never shows a completed duel where Itachi applies it successfully to Madara. Madara is a highly experienced Uchiha ocular-jutsu user; assuming he would casually walk into an unknown eye trap is not a strong basis for a verdict. Nor can we declare a universal immunity without evidence of the exact interaction.

Even a plausible illusion would have to be applied before Madara's scale changes the battle. Against an opponent who can attack through clones and massive destructive techniques, Itachi may not get the controlled one-on-one visual exchange he prefers. A possible effect under ideal conditions is different from a likely result under typical ones. This is the main analytical distinction: Itachi has tools that can cause serious consequences, but Madara has more ways to prevent him from reaching the point where those tools can be used decisively.
Itachi vs Madara: could the Totsuka Blade seal him?

The Totsuka Blade is the most interesting route to a possible upset. Its sealing power could matter greatly against a reanimated enemy because ordinary damage is not always a permanent solution. Yet an attack having a decisive effect when it lands tells us nothing about whether it can reach this particular opponent. Itachi would need to deliver a strike through Madara's offense and defenses, potentially while distinguishing the real Madara from multiple dangerous clones.

The war-arc evidence makes that obstacle enormous. Madara's Susanoo-capable wood clones and Perfect Susanoo show how much space and pressure he can control. We cannot claim Itachi's blade would automatically pass through all of that, just as we cannot dismiss sealing as irrelevant in principle. Our view is that a hypothetical Itachi victory requires a very specific and unshown contact scenario, while Madara has numerous demonstrated paths to pressure or defeat him. That strongly favors Madara without erasing the theoretical threat.
Itachi vs Madara: living, Edo Tensei and Ten-Tails forms

Madara's power changes substantially across the story. Historical living Madara has immense experience and extraordinary Uchiha abilities. Reanimated Madara demonstrates the arsenal that overwhelms the Allied Shinobi Forces and Kage. Later he becomes the Ten-Tails jinchuriki and faces opponents empowered by the Sage of Six Paths. These are not minor costume changes. They alter his endurance, scale and possible defenses in ways that must be specified when comparing him with another fighter.

Against war-era reanimated Madara, we strongly favor Madara. Against Ten-Tails Madara, the gap grows even larger. Restricting the comparison to some earlier Madara version may produce a more nuanced conversation, but it cannot legitimately borrow feats from his final transformation while denying that the transformation is being used. The same fairness applies to Itachi: giving him an immortal reanimated body requires saying so openly. The two characters can both be admired without pretending that their strongest demonstrated battlefields are equivalent.
Our four-matchup scorecard, without invented odds

Itachi versus masked Obito: no definitive canon duel; conditional edge to Obito because Kamui prevents reliable contact, with a prepared Itachi potentially able to exploit a forced opening. Itachi versus Kakashi: early direct encounter won by Itachi's Tsukuyomi. War-era Kakashi: unresolved hypothetical, with Kamui providing serious counterplay. Temporary DMS Kakashi: conditional edge to Kakashi in that exceptional late-war form.

Itachi versus living Minato: no definitive canon duel; conditional edge to Minato for Flying Raijin's control of distance, while Itachi remains dangerous through genjutsu and a sealing hit. Itachi versus reanimated or Ten-Tails Madara: no definitive canon duel; strong advantage to Madara because his documented resources and scale dwarf those seen in Itachi's ordinary fights. We avoid imaginary ninety-nine-percent predictions. The evidence supports broad leanings more readily than exact probabilities.
Three scenarios that make the debate more useful

First is an unprepared meeting. Both characters recognize the other as dangerous but do not know all the details of their opponent's abilities. That gives unusual importance to the first encounter and the ability to learn without being punished. Second is a prepared duel in which both know the relevant techniques and can position themselves. Itachi can design misleading openings, Minato can distribute marks and Obito can plan an approach. The third is a mission with a defined objective: capture, seal, survive or force a retreat rather than simply kill.

A reader can make the comparison more rigorous by writing down the character versions, starting distance, preparation, available outside assistance and what counts as victory. If the explanation depends on Obito voluntarily standing still, Kakashi ignoring an obvious illusion, Minato forgetting his markers or Madara refusing to use his clones, the scenario may be doing all the work. A good hypothetical should allow both fighters to behave intelligently, not only the reader's favorite.
Five familiar claims that need more care

The first is that Sharingan ownership gives universal Tsukuyomi immunity; Kakashi's early encounter shows that eye users can have radically different capabilities. The second is that Kamui makes Obito eternally untouchable, when the official war story documents a dimensional interaction and an opening. The third is that Minato's teleportation automatically protects his mind. The fourth is that the Totsuka Blade wins as soon as someone mentions it, ignoring the challenge of getting a sealing strike to land.

The fifth is that the word Susanoo makes Itachi and Madara equals, regardless of size, clones and other techniques. An additional problem is the healthy Itachi hypothetical. Removing his illness can be an interesting thought experiment, but the manga never displays a fully documented alternate career in which his chakra, stamina and every battle outcome can be measured. Calling that form canon does not make the argument stronger. Naruto rewards careful attention to conditions, even when fans would prefer a simpler result.
Why these matchups reveal different sides of Itachi

Obito tests Itachi's ability to force contact against someone who can appear to leave the physical world. Kakashi tests whether learning and experience can reverse an earlier defeat. Minato tests the value of choosing the precise instant and location of an exchange. Madara tests how far cleverness can go when an opponent commands overwhelming area-wide resources. Each pairing therefore tells readers something different about fighting styles, rather than providing four excuses to repeat that Itachi has a sealing sword.

There is a character story beneath the techniques, too. Itachi spends much of his life controlling what others believe and making plans for how they should act. Naruto reveals the terrible limits of that approach through Sasuke's response to the truth. His best hypothetical matchups are similarly interesting when the plan can fail. He might read a habit brilliantly, misjudge a teleportation or create an elegant trap that an opponent refuses to enter. Intelligent fighters remain fallible, and admitting that makes the debate more faithful to the source material.
Frequently asked questions about all four fights

Did Itachi defeat Kakashi? Yes, in their early encounter he incapacitates Kakashi with Tsukuyomi. Did Itachi ever beat Obito, Minato or Madara in a definitive canonical duel? No such completed one-on-one result establishes those wins. Does DMS Kakashi mean Itachi's earlier victory never mattered? No; that is a later temporary form that changes the terms. Could Itachi catch Obito in Tsukuyomi? It is a possible hypothetical opening, not a demonstrated canonical result against Obito. Could Minato teleport out of Tsukuyomi? His teleportation does not by itself establish immunity to an illusion once applied.

Would a perfectly healthy Itachi beat Madara? The story does not provide a fully shown healthy endgame Itachi with measurable alternate feats, and late-war Madara still has a commanding display of power. Could Itachi's Totsuka Blade seal an opponent who is already reanimated? Its sealing role is relevant, but successful contact remains the issue in a hypothetical. Which pairing has the strongest source-backed answer? Itachi versus early Kakashi, because Naruto actually depicts the decisive genjutsu exchange. Why are the other conclusions conditional? Because one missing battle cannot be made into a recorded fact by confidently imagining it.
How these conclusions were checked

We used Naruto's official retrospective of Itachi, the original anime episode listing for the Kakashi encounter, the Great Ninja War accounts of Kamui and the Five Kage battle, official explanations of Flying Raijin, and official coverage of Madara's transformations and temporary double-Mangekyo Kakashi. The retrospectives connect much of the discussion to recognizable original manga chapters, which can be checked through authorized editions such as VIZ's English Naruto catalog.

Those official materials establish the techniques and events. They do not declare official winners for the three unshown duels or for Kakashi's alternative later forms. Our verdicts are editorial interpretations of what the techniques make possible, with uncertainty wherever the franchise leaves an interaction unresolved. If you want to challenge one, begin by naming the exact version, the battlefield and the mechanism of your preferred winning move. That makes a better discussion than a ranking copied from a thumbnail.

title: Was Itachi a Hero or Villain? The Hardest Moral Question in Naruto
description: Was Itachi good or evil? A balanced look at his motives, the Uchiha victims, Sasuke's trauma, Danzō's role and why his final confession still matters.
keywords: was Itachi a hero or villain, is Itachi good or evil Naruto, was Itachi right, Itachi Uchiha moral analysis, why is Itachi a hero, Itachi sacrificed for village, Itachi Sasuke love flaws
summary: Itachi is written as a tragic character with protective motives who still commits devastating acts. He acted under coercive political pressure to avert a coup and preserve Sasuke's life, but the massacre, secrecy and psychological harm cannot be made harmless by the late revelation. The story ultimately asks us to weigh duty and love against agency, victims and consequences—not to issue an official hero-or-villain score.

sections: The question matters because the answer is uncomfortable

Itachi is one of Naruto's most discussed characters because the story gives us two portraits that seem impossible to hold together. In one, he is the older brother who destroys his clan and deliberately wounds the only family member he leaves alive. In the other, he is a frightened young shinobi who fears war, loves his brother and accepts an unbearable burden to prevent a greater catastrophe. Neither portrait is simply fake. The tension between them is what makes Itachi more than a puzzle with a secret solution.

This article is not an attempt to tell readers which emotion they should feel. It is a way to examine an important distinction: an explanation for an act is not a moral pardon for that act. Naruto provides strong evidence for Itachi's protective motives and for the coercive environment that shaped his choices. It also shows enormous harm. An honest hero-or-villain discussion has to begin by admitting both and by keeping the victims visible even when the narrative later moves toward his final confession.
A young boy learns to hate the idea of war

The official Naruto biography follows Itachi back to his experience of battlefield death at a very young age. He is not attracted to violence for its own sake. He imagines a world in which people do not have to repeat the same destruction that shaped his earliest understanding of being a shinobi. This is an unusually sympathetic starting point for a character who will eventually be feared as an international criminal. It tells us that violence and compassion are not distributed neatly among Naruto's heroes and enemies.

His talent complicates the situation. Adults read his exceptional ability as evidence that he can carry responsibilities other children cannot. His clan wants a skilled insider; the village security apparatus wants a useful observer. Itachi begins to inhabit roles that demand obedience before he possesses the authority to change the conditions that make those roles necessary. Calling him a child soldier is an analytical description of this dynamic, not a claim that the franchise uses that specific legal label. He is drawn into an institution that repeatedly turns youth into instruments.
The strongest argument for seeing Itachi as a tragic protector

Itachi hopes to prevent a violent Uchiha uprising from bringing civil war to Konoha, and his loyalty to Sasuke is not invented after the fact. The official Naruto column carefully describes that bond through childhood gestures and the final battle. Itachi understands that opposing the clan will destroy his standing among the people who should have been closest to him. He accepts the identity of a monster because he thinks that story can preserve the village and leave Sasuke a future.

He also demonstrates a willingness to take the blame personally rather than seek public recognition as someone who saved Konoha. That willingness explains why so many viewers experience the final revelation as tragic rather than simply manipulative. He gives up his reputation and eventually his life for an idea of peace. In a world where power so often becomes a demand for glory, the refusal to be praised is meaningful. But sacrifice can be sincere even when the chosen method is morally disastrous.
The strongest argument against calling him a hero

The massacre is not a metaphor. People die, including people who were not the architects of the coup. Itachi kills members of his own family while acting through a political project that would never be tolerable if we were assessing it only by its consequences. The facts that he suffered and was pressured do not erase the suffering of others. Any moral evaluation that discusses only what he surrendered and never what was taken from those who died is fundamentally unbalanced.

Sasuke's survival does not cancel the harm to him either. Itachi lets him grow up under a false understanding, and the narrative shows the damage caused by years of hatred and mental torment. The plan requires Sasuke to make a terrible mistake about the world and then build his identity around correcting it. Even when motivated by protection, this is control. The later confession can explain why Itachi behaved as he did, but it cannot give Sasuke back an untraumatized childhood.
Danzō and the village: when an institution needs a scapegoat

Danzō's influence belongs at the center of this moral accounting because the crisis was not a private argument between siblings. The village tolerated political mistrust and empowered secret actors who treated atrocity as a tool of security. The Uchiha's plan for an armed coup was itself dangerous; that does not make collective slaughter a justified answer. The official Naruto and Shisui materials together make clear that a possible intervention was undermined and the security response hardened into catastrophic violence.

It is too easy to praise Itachi's selflessness while leaving the institutions that used him untouched. That is what the story quietly warns against. A talented person who accepts guilt on behalf of the state may look noble to observers, while the state retains the ability to recruit the next person for a similar act. Naruto's wider interest in inherited conflict gives this problem long reach. Sasuke's later anger at Konoha may be destructive, but it is not incomprehensible once he knows who paid for the village's stability.
The decision tree the story never lets us observe

One way to judge the character fairly is to distinguish choices from outcomes. Itachi could imagine a coup followed by civil war, and he was given a violently narrow menu of alternatives. Those beliefs help explain his decisions. But readers are not shown a parallel version of the story in which negotiation succeeded, or one in which every combatant refused Danzō. No amount of confident fandom debate can turn those counterfactual scenarios into canonical footage.

This limits two common arguments. 'There was absolutely no other possible way' is stronger than the evidence permits. 'He could easily have solved it all peacefully' is also an invention unless someone supplies the process, risks and people required. The more grounded moral point is that a system which corners a young subordinate into choosing between mass violence and anticipated mass violence has already failed. Itachi's individual guilt and the system's responsibility belong in the same discussion.
Did Itachi protect Sasuke—or try to write his life for him?

The clearest evidence of Itachi's love comes through action, not just speeches. The official retrospective recalls small everyday gestures toward Sasuke as a child, his concern over the curse mark and the final moment after their battle. Those details justify saying his attachment was real. But love in Naruto often becomes dangerous when it is mixed with the desire to determine another person's future. Itachi wants Sasuke to live, but also wants him to become a particular kind of avenger and later defender.

When the truth comes out, Sasuke's response shatters that plan. He does not accept the first story he was told, yet he cannot simply return to the innocent world that existed before it. His anger changes direction. This failure is essential to the moral reading of Itachi: if his plan had worked perfectly, the story might look like praise for sacrificing one life to control another. Instead, it shows how a protective intention can become a new source of harm when it denies the protected person knowledge and choice.
His final conversation changes the moral relationship

During the Fourth Great Ninja War, reanimated Itachi gets a final chance to speak with Sasuke. That scene matters because it is different in purpose from his earlier manipulations. Rather than stage another illusion about who Sasuke should hate, he tells him the truth and accepts that his brother may never forgive him. The Naruto official war-arc account places this beside Sasuke's subsequent decision to think for himself about the world and his path forward.

That is a profound change, though not a retroactive repair of the past. Itachi finally gives up the project of authoring Sasuke's life. He recognizes that loving someone and controlling their future are not the same thing. The most meaningful part of the farewell is not a clever technique or an added revelation about his power. It is the acceptance that Sasuke has the right to respond in his own way. In a story filled with cycles of revenge, that small surrender of control can be as important as any battlefield victory.
Our moral scorecard: motives, means, costs and lessons

Motives: Itachi sought to prevent war and preserve Sasuke, goals that are understandable and in themselves defensible. Means: he participated in the annihilation of his own clan and orchestrated psychological deception, actions that cause severe harm. Costs: the Uchiha lost lives, Sasuke lost his family and Itachi forfeited the possibility of an ordinary life. Consequences: the immediate political threat ends, but Sasuke's trauma and the village's buried guilt continue to shape the wider story.

That balance sheet is more illuminating than a score of ninety percent hero or ten percent villain. It separates the dimensions that readers are otherwise asked to collapse. The story supports sympathy for someone who was used by powerful institutions. It does not require admiration for what he did to vulnerable people. It also supports anger toward those institutions without proving that any particular alternative timeline would have been painless. A mature character reading can hold those conclusions simultaneously.
Why viewers keep returning to Itachi years later

Many beloved anime characters are memorable because they become stronger. Itachi is memorable because new information makes older scenes feel different. A cold expression can become resignation; an apparent attack can be part of a grim contingency; a seemingly final gesture can recover a memory of childhood. The reveal invites a rewatch, not simply a revised opinion of his power. That is a structural achievement in storytelling.

There is also a recognizable human problem underneath the supernatural abilities: what happens when a person is praised for bearing a secret that should never have been theirs? The official VIZ introduction to Itachi's Daylight novel frames him through the drastically different ways people perceived him—criminal, weapon, hope and lost brother. Each perspective contains a part of his story and misses something essential. The reason the argument continues is that Naruto never allows a single reputation to account for all the damage and love.
Questions without a simplistic verdict

Was Itachi secretly good? He had protective motives and a capacity for love, but that does not make every action good. Is he a villain in Naruto? For much of the story he functions as an antagonist; later revelations deliberately complicate that role. Was the massacre his idea alone? The wider coup and Danzō's coercive security response are essential factors. Did Sasuke forgive him? Their final meeting is a form of emotional reconciliation, but Itachi explicitly makes space for Sasuke not to absolve him.

Can fans reasonably admire Itachi and still condemn the massacre? Yes. Those views are not contradictory when admiration concerns his courage, intelligence or self-criticism rather than endorsement of mass killing. Did Naruto officially declare an ethical winner? No. Itachi's arc works because the story's strongest emotional gesture is not a verdict from a judge; it is a brother finally allowing another brother to choose for himself. That is where our interpretation ends and yours can begin.

sections: There are two good watch orders, and they serve different viewers

Searching for the Itachi episodes can be surprisingly frustrating. One guide recommends a childhood flashback first; another starts with the famous brother-versus-brother battle; a third lists an episode number that appears far beyond the end of some US streaming seasons. None of these is necessarily malicious. The confusion comes from different goals and numbering systems, as well as the fact that Itachi's motives were deliberately hidden when the audience first met him.

Choose the route by your situation. If you are watching Naruto for the first time, follow the main story order. Itachi works as a mystery because Sasuke's version of him comes first. If you already know the major twist, a focused Itachi rewatch can move chronologically through childhood, the massacre, Akatsuki, the duel and the war. If you prefer reading, the original Naruto manga and the separately published Itachi novels give you another route. This guide separates those choices instead of claiming one list is perfect for everyone.
First-time viewers: preserve the mystery

The least frustrating spoiler-safe route is the ordinary progression from Naruto into Naruto Shippuden. That lets you meet Itachi through Kakashi's frightening encounter, Sasuke's reaction and the developing mystery of the Akatsuki. His apparent cruelty is part of how Naruto tells the story. Watching the backstory adaptation first would explain hidden motives before the characters have earned the truth, changing the impact of scenes that depend on uncertainty.

At this stage it is better to resist compilations titled The Full Truth About Itachi. They often contain unmarked footage of the massacre, his final fight and his war-arc farewell. Those scenes may be beautiful, but they reveal key story turns years before a first-time viewer reaches them. If you want a small preview, use official introductory character material rather than an algorithm-driven edit that jumps between decades of story chronology. The point is to encounter the mystery in the order it was written.
For returning fans: a five-stage Itachi story route

An effective rewatch divides the material into five stages. First comes childhood and the political crisis, where Itachi's ideals form and his relationship with Shisui becomes central. Second is the massacre and departure into the Akatsuki. Third comes his role as a threat in the original Naruto era and as a distant figure influencing Sasuke's choices. Fourth is the final brothers' fight and the revelation of its hidden context. Fifth is his reanimated return, cooperation with Sasuke and last farewell during the Fourth Great Ninja War.

This is a story path rather than a promise that each phase fits one season block. The episodes are interleaved with Naruto's much wider ensemble plot. In a rewatch, that is an advantage: you can follow Itachi's personal arc while remembering that the world did not stop moving between his appearances. But if you are new, use this progression only after you are comfortable knowing why he joined Akatsuki and what happened to the Uchiha.
Where does the Itachi Shinden arc begin?

On common Naruto Shippuden episode listings in the United States, the Itachi Shinden: Light and Darkness flashback runs across episodes 451–458. The installments include Birth and Death, The Genius, The Pain of Living, Shisui's Request, Moonlit Night, The Darkness of the Akatsuki, Partner and Truth. Licensed Google Play listings present this sequence under Shippuden episode numbers. These names are useful when a service splits the show into unusual season packs or omits the numbering entirely.

The official Naruto franchise website uses a different numbering system on its English anime archive. It lists the same Itachi's Story: Daylight / Midnight arc as episodes 671–678 because that index numbers Naruto and Shippuden episodes across a combined sequence. It does not mean there are two different eight-episode Itachi arcs. You can verify that the opening Birth and Death installment appears as official index episode 671 while a US listing calls it Shippuden episode 451. Both point to the same story.
What is actually in those eight episodes?

The arc follows Itachi as a gifted child confronted by the cost of war, then shows his training and his attempts to navigate clan and village politics. Shisui is especially important because the story gives the pair time together before the crisis destroys their shared plan. The later episodes connect Itachi's ANBU role, Danzō's influence, the Uchiha coup and the night of the massacre. Afterward, the series turns toward his relationships within Akatsuki and the fractured connection to Sasuke.

The sequence is useful because it lets the audience live with the consequences in ordinary scenes rather than learn everything from one later explanation. Still, the official anime index labels this arc anime-original. The episodes draw from a larger body of franchise material but are not a word-for-word reproduction of the original manga or both novels. If you want to discuss specific dialogue or details, identify whether you mean the manga, the novels or the television adaptation; the distinctions matter.
When should you watch the brothers' decisive fight?

The emotional center of Itachi's story is his confrontation with Sasuke late in the latter's pursuit of revenge. It belongs in the main Shippuden progression, after Sasuke has spent years becoming the person Itachi wanted him to be. The battle itself includes genjutsu exchanges, increasingly dangerous attacks and an ending whose meaning changes dramatically when the next stage of the story reveals Itachi's background.

Rather than give a single season number—which differs sharply by service—follow the official Naruto Master's Prophecy and Vengeance arc and the manga's corresponding material in volumes 42–44. The Naruto official retrospective identifies the brothers' confrontation and the relevant chapters. This route protects readers from landing on the wrong episode because a streaming platform calls one part Season 8 while another service calls the same segment something different. Look for the arc and title, then verify the episode on your platform.
Do not skip the war-arc farewell

The original duel does not conclude everything Itachi has to say. His reanimated return during the war brings him into contact with Naruto and Killer Bee, then with Sasuke again. The brothers cooperate against Kabuto to undo the Reanimation Jutsu, giving them a brief chance to act as allies instead of enemies. This second encounter is essential to understanding how Itachi finally addresses the truth he kept hidden and how Sasuke makes his next decision.

The official Naruto episode index includes I Will Love You Always as episode 559 in the all-franchise sequence. The matching main-story placement can be located through the Great Ninja War: Sasuke and Itachi arc; pay attention to the arc title if your streaming provider renumbers it. This is why a viewing list that stops at the original death is incomplete. Itachi's final moments in the war do not magically undo his earlier actions, but they mark a shift from trying to steer Sasuke to allowing him to choose.
Reading Naruto: manga first or supplemental novels?

Masashi Kishimoto's Naruto manga is the cleanest foundation for the main canon narrative. The official Naruto birthday retrospect cites chapter and volume locations for key Itachi scenes, including the Uchiha political revelation in volume 43 and the later final farewell in volume 62. Those references are far more helpful than random image boards of isolated panels. VIZ provides an authorized English catalog for readers in the United States, with chapter and volume access governed by its own offerings.

VIZ also publishes Naruto: Itachi's Story: Daylight and Midnight. Its Daylight introduction describes Itachi's early experience of war and the layers of loyalty that make him difficult to judge. The novels add an extended perspective that differs in presentation from the main manga; the anime's adaptation also makes its own choices. We would not advise treating every anime-only scene as an interchangeable statement of manga fact. For a reader who wants the deepest view, read the manga's central reveal first, then use the two novels for context and comparison.
Spoiler levels: which route is safe for you?

There are three useful levels. Level one: you have just met Itachi and know only that Sasuke hates him. Stay with the main series. Level two: you have finished the brothers' fight and learned the political truth. You can watch the Itachi Shinden flashback without losing the big reveal, though it may still introduce details from much later in Shippuden. Level three: you have reached the Fourth Great Ninja War. Now the entire character route—including Shisui's crow, Izanami and the final farewell—can be revisited without accidentally reading ahead.

These levels are an editorial convenience, not official content labels. They help readers decide what sort of knowledge they want before clicking. This is better than classifying a whole eight-episode arc as harmless filler and telling new fans to skip it or watch it first. Filler labels describe adaptation origin, not whether something carries emotional value. Itachi's flashbacks can be worthwhile precisely because they spend time on experiences the main story compresses.
The US viewing question: why can't one platform link solve this?

Streaming services license anime by region, package episodes differently and sometimes divide English dubbing into separate availability windows. A screenshot of one catalog is therefore not proof that every US subscriber can watch an episode in that arrangement. Search the official title page for Naruto Shippuden and confirm the series, audio choice and installment title. If the visible listing says 671 while your app ends Shippuden at 500, the difference may be the combined official franchise counter rather than a missing episode.

Do not confuse a retail availability listing with a blanket statement about subscription streaming. Google Play, VIZ and other authorized services have distinct models, and the legal availability of one episode can change. Our numbered guide describes where the story appears, not a guarantee that a particular package is free or included today. It is worth taking a minute to check rather than purchasing a season that begins after the scene you actually wanted.
Quick Itachi episode and reading questions

Are Shippuden episodes 451–458 worth watching? For fans who want the character's upbringing, Shisui relationship and political background, yes; but first-time viewers may prefer to save them for after the central reveal. Why does the official Naruto site say 671–678? Its index combines Naruto and Shippuden numbering, while US platforms commonly number Shippuden alone. Do the VIZ novels equal these episodes? No. They are related licensed prose works, not duplicate files of the broadcast scripts.

Can I watch only the Itachi scenes? You can, but Sasuke's long emotional development and the politics of Konoha will be harder to understand. Does the story end when Itachi first dies? No; the war arc returns him through reanimation for a second farewell. What is the spoiler-safe starting point? Begin with the original Naruto series and continue in its release-story sequence. That is still the most rewarding way to discover who Itachi was before reading an explanation.

sections: Two friends who were trying to solve the same problem

Itachi and Shisui are often remembered as a pair of exceptionally powerful Uchiha with tragic stories. That shorthand misses the reason their relationship matters. They were trying to prevent a political confrontation from becoming a massacre. Shisui imagined a possible intervention that would stop the coup without killing the clan, while Itachi feared the violence gathering on both sides. Their friendship developed from training and mutual trust into shared responsibility for a crisis that grown leaders failed to resolve.

The official Naruto Shisui birthday column gives us an unusually clear evidence trail. It names their friendship, explains the ability of Kotoamatsukami, records the seizure of one eye, and follows the other eye all the way to Itachi's unexpected liberation during the war. This article traces that chain without assuming every supplementary anime scene is identical to the manga. The story is spoiler-heavy for the Uchiha massacre and the Fourth Great Ninja War.
Who was Shisui to Itachi?

Shisui was more than another talented clan member. He was a close friend whom Itachi looked up to as an older brother figure. Their relationship offered something Itachi rarely found elsewhere: a person with whom he could discuss the demands of loyalty without pretending that the village and clan were always right. They trained together, questioned what it meant to be a shinobi and saw the growing danger in the Uchiha political conflict. A younger Itachi found a kind of moral companion before the choices around him became catastrophic.

That history is easy to overlook if you enter Naruto through brief clips of Shisui's eyes. His importance is not reducible to the genjutsu he possessed. He represented the possibility that power could be used to de-escalate rather than dominate. The anime's Itachi Shinden episodes expand their time together, while the official franchise column points back to manga chapters showing the friendship and its consequences. Both are useful, but they tell the story through different emphases.
What is Kotoamatsukami?

Kotoamatsukami is Shisui's exceptionally subtle genjutsu. Unlike an illusion that obviously changes the scenery or traps someone in a visible nightmare, it can influence thoughts and intentions so that the target experiences the resulting decision as their own. The official Naruto profile describes the manipulation as capable of passing unnoticed. That makes it terrifying in a political crisis: a person's apparent agreement might be genuine persuasion—or a choice secretly planted through an ocular technique.

The ability also introduces a moral puzzle. Shisui's purpose was to prevent bloodshed. But changing a leader's mind without that leader knowing it has happened is not ordinary negotiation. Even when the desired outcome is peace, the method erases the target's independent consent. Naruto uses extraordinary powers to make familiar ethical problems difficult to ignore. If stopping a violent coup requires making someone believe a thought that was never theirs, how different is that from the coercion the heroes say they oppose?
Why did Danzō take Shisui's eye?

Danzō did not trust the proposed intervention. According to the official retrospective, he seized Shisui's right eye during the effort to prevent the coup. That removed an important tool Shisui hoped to use and left the young shinobi with narrowing alternatives. It also showed how people charged with protecting the village could treat the bodies and abilities of their own allies as resources to seize. The episode is not just one villain acquiring a powerful item; it is a political move that damages any chance of solving the crisis without force.

Fans sometimes describe this incident as a clean debate between Shisui's flawless peace plan and Danzō's inevitable massacre. It was neither. Kotoamatsukami's own coercive nature creates uncomfortable questions, and the story does not give us a demonstrated alternate timeline in which its use solves everything permanently. What is shown is that Danzō's action undermines an attempted alternative and deepens the tragedy. Itachi is left carrying a trust that the institution has already betrayed.
Why did Shisui give Itachi his remaining eye?

After losing the right eye, Shisui entrusts his remaining eye to Itachi and places his hopes for the village and Uchiha future with him. His death is the breaking point in Itachi's life, closely tied to the awakening of Itachi's Mangekyō Sharingan. It is important not to turn the event into a convenient power-up story. A friend dies, a possible peaceful intervention disappears and a young person is pushed further toward a decision he finds intolerable.

Shisui's gift also must be tracked correctly. The right eye taken by Danzō and the left eye given to Itachi are not the same physical object moving through one uninterrupted chain of owners. Many simplified explainers collapse them into a single magical eye that 'went from Danzō to Naruto.' That is wrong. The official column makes the two routes clear. Keeping them separate answers much of the apparent mystery that follows.
Why did Itachi put a crow inside Naruto?

Years later Itachi uses a crow as a way of carrying Shisui's surviving eye and its Kotoamatsukami ability. He places this safeguard with Naruto, who is determined to bring Sasuke back from his destructive path. Itachi expects that Sasuke may eventually become dangerous to Konoha and wants a contingency that might redirect him without simply killing him. The choice is deeply revealing. Even from outside the village, Itachi is trying to manage Sasuke's future through another person's intervention.

One should resist the temptation to describe the crow as a constant all-purpose guardian that can independently solve whatever problem arises. It is a highly specific arrangement with a particular trigger and an important eye technique. Naruto does not receive a permanent inventory of Itachi's powers. Instead, he unknowingly carries a safeguard whose eventual activation takes place in conditions Itachi did not originally intend. That difference is what makes its later appearance dramatic.
What happened when the crow appeared during the war?

After Kabuto reanimates Itachi, Naruto and Killer Bee encounter the revived Uchiha and Nagato. The crow emerges from Naruto and Kotoamatsukami acts on Itachi rather than Sasuke. The effect overrides the control exerted by the Reanimation Jutsu, leaving Itachi free to act on his own. The official Naruto anniversary account explicitly traces this sequence. It is an astonishing reversal: a technique meant to restrain a possible future version of Sasuke instead frees the man who arranged it.

This is not the same as Kotoamatsukami instantly defeating Kabuto. The technique releases Itachi from one form of control; Itachi must still work out how to confront the source of the reanimation and end the jutsu. He goes on to cooperate with Sasuke against Kabuto. The eye has fulfilled a protective purpose, but not the one assigned to it in the original plan. A strategy that depended on controlling Sasuke becomes, unexpectedly, a way for Itachi to correct some of his own mistakes.
A simple eye-by-eye record that avoids the common myths

Start with the right eye: Danzō seizes it from Shisui. Its later significance is tied to the schemes and power of Danzō himself. Then follow the left eye: Shisui entrusts it to Itachi; Itachi preserves its power in a crow associated with Naruto; the crow activates when reanimated Itachi meets Naruto and frees him from Kabuto's command. Those are two separate routes. Keeping the record this simple is more useful than any complicated drawing filled with speculative transfers.

Next separate native abilities from borrowed ones. Itachi's Tsukuyomi and Amaterasu are associated with his own Mangekyō powers. Kotoamatsukami is Shisui's distinctive technique, available later through the preserved eye. Finally separate intention from outcome: the eye's first purpose was a contingency for Sasuke, while its actual decisive use concerns Itachi. These three distinctions clear up the most persistent confusion around the crow without inventing extra rules.
Was Shisui's plan morally better than Itachi's?

Shisui sought an alternative to killing the clan; in that obvious sense, his stated objective was less catastrophic. But a plan to influence a person's mind without awareness is still ethically troubling. Itachi's eventual massacre is worse in its scale and irreversible harm. The story's richness comes from refusing to make secret power the easy solution to a crisis produced by ordinary discrimination, fear and political control.

Both young shinobi were trying to repair a system from the inside while leaders with more authority acted to preserve their own position. Their abilities were remarkable, but neither possessed the institutional power to guarantee an honest settlement. Reading the events as a contest between the best genjutsu and the strongest political faction misses that difference. The deepest tragedy is how readily people entrusted a problem of governance to children carrying weapons.
Quick answers about Shisui and the crow

Did Shisui die before the Uchiha massacre? Yes, his death occurs during the rising crisis before the fateful night. Did Danzō take both eyes? No; Shisui's remaining eye was entrusted to Itachi. Is Kotoamatsukami Itachi's natural Mangekyō technique? No, the technique belongs to Shisui and is used later through Shisui's preserved eye. Why did it activate on Itachi? The contingency was triggered during the reanimated encounter with Naruto, producing an unintended but decisive result.

Did the crow make Itachi permanently alive? No. He remained a reanimated shinobi who later departed when the technique was undone. Could the original peace plan definitely have prevented the massacre? The story never shows that alternate future. The dependable reference points are the official Shisui birthday column and the official Great Ninja War retrospective, which together record the two eye routes and the later activation.

sections: Itachi is powerful because he changes the terms of a fight

Itachi Uchiha is commonly introduced through images of red eyes and the Akatsuki cloak, but that iconography hides a more interesting skill set. He does not simply hit harder than the person standing opposite him. He controls attention, creates false information, makes opponents doubt what they experienced and forces them to react to threats that may already have decided the battle. This is why early encounters with Itachi feel so different from a conventional contest of punches and chakra.

This guide explains his signature techniques in plain language, including the conditions that make them powerful and the limitations the story shows. It discusses events through the brothers' battle and the Fourth Great Ninja War, so later sections contain spoilers. The core distinction to keep in mind is that the regular Sharingan, Mangekyō Sharingan, Susanoo and forbidden techniques do not all work the same way. Calling everything 'Itachi's eye power' hides the decisions that make his fights intelligent.
The regular Sharingan: seeing, anticipating and deceiving

The Uchiha Sharingan supports heightened visual perception and the ability to read or anticipate an opponent's movements. That does not mean it grants literal knowledge of every future event. The eye helps its user process important details very quickly; the person still has to make judgments. Itachi combines that capacity with disciplined movement, shuriken technique and a remarkable talent for genjutsu. He often makes a fight look easier because he has shaped the opponent's choices before the decisive exchange.

The more easily overlooked ability is deception. A thrown weapon, a clone or a brief change in eye contact can turn into a test of what the opponent trusts. The official Naruto retrospective of the Sasuke duel describes apparent injuries that prove to be layered illusions. In that kind of encounter the audience shares the combatant's uncertainty. The lesson is not that Sharingan defeats every fighter. It is that allowing Itachi to dictate the information you act on gives him an immense strategic advantage.
Tsukuyomi: a mental attack that distorts experienced time

Tsukuyomi is associated with Itachi's Mangekyō Sharingan and is among his most frightening techniques because it attacks perception itself. The victim is pulled into an illusion where time and suffering can feel radically different from their duration outside. Kakashi's encounter makes the danger visible: Itachi traps him in an exhausting mental ordeal while the real-world moment is brief. A reader who thinks genjutsu merely means seeing a harmless false picture will miss how serious the consequences can be.

The technique's value comes from its speed and mental pressure, not from causing the largest environmental explosion. It also explains why veterans warn against meeting Itachi's gaze. Yet a prohibition on looking into his eyes is not a complete counter to every move he possesses, and eye-contact strategies depend on the opponent and situation. Tsukuyomi has specific conditions and can be resisted in particular circumstances. The exact rules should be read through demonstrated scenes rather than a fan-invented promise of unconditional control.
Amaterasu: black flames that change the battlefield

Amaterasu manifests as intensely destructive black flames. It is easy to see why fans talk about it as if an unavoidable finishing move had been added to every confrontation. On the page or screen, however, targeting, reaction, movement, defense and the consequences of hitting the environment all matter. The power forces an opponent to solve an urgent positional problem, often making escape or interruption a priority rather than direct attack.

In the fight with Sasuke, Amaterasu shifts the duel from mental trickery to visibly escalating physical danger. That change in scale is part of the drama. But a spectacular attack does not establish that Itachi can hit anyone in any location at any distance with no limitation. Naruto repeatedly depicts unusual defenses, replacements and specialized responses to techniques that initially seem decisive. It is more accurate to call Amaterasu an extraordinary offensive ability whose effectiveness depends on whether the target can be engaged under the right conditions.
Susanoo: protection, weapons and its own demands

Susanoo gives Itachi a giant chakra-based defensive and offensive manifestation. Its appearance changes the matchup because Itachi can withstand attacks that would otherwise reach his body and employ special weapons from behind that protection. In the brothers' battle, it is crucial to his survival of Sasuke's devastating lightning technique. The defensive value is obvious, but it would be a mistake to read that one survival as proof that no power in the Naruto world can ever bypass or outlast Susanoo.

Susanoo is also demanding, particularly for a fighter whose health is already failing. Itachi can use it in extraordinary moments; he cannot treat it as a costless wall that stays active indefinitely in every imagined battle. A useful power guide must ask whether the technique is active, how long its user can sustain it, what the opponent can do to change the situation and whether the user's goals permit a direct finishing attempt. That is where an interesting hypothetical starts, rather than where it ends.
The Totsuka Blade and Yata Mirror are not generic equipment

Itachi's Susanoo is associated with the Totsuka Blade, a sealing weapon, and the Yata Mirror, a defensive shield-like treasure. These are not ordinary metal items that he buys or carries into every mission. They belong to the legendary spiritual arsenal of his Susanoo. The blade matters especially when Orochimaru's power manifests during the Sasuke confrontation; Itachi's response removes a dangerous influence from his brother's future.

The Yata Mirror's reputation leads to exaggerated statements that Itachi's whole body is permanently untouchable from every direction. The more grounded interpretation is that a remarkable defensive tool is shown within the technique. A skilled opponent still has meaningful questions to ask about angle, timing, duration and resource exhaustion. The same applies to the Totsuka Blade: a sealing effect is formidable if it makes contact, but the story does not provide evidence that any opponent can be hit whenever Itachi wishes.
Izanami: Itachi's most revealing technique

Izanami is the strange finishing technique Itachi uses during the confrontation with Kabuto. Rather than overwhelming Kabuto with a larger flame or stronger sword, it traps him in a repeating loop of experience and confronts him with his refusal to acknowledge reality. Its narrative function is different from a straightforward destructive attack. It acts on a pattern of behavior, and the escape condition is tied to the target's acceptance of what they are.

The cost is also severe: the forbidden eye technique sacrifices the vision of the eye used. The official Naruto anniversary account describes how it is prepared and employed against Kabuto to secure the undoing of the Reanimation Jutsu. Reducing Izanami to 'Itachi instantly defeats anyone forever' ignores its setup, purpose and price. A technique with an extraordinary outcome can remain limited by circumstance, preparation and the user's willingness to pay the cost.
Do not confuse Izanami with Izanagi or Kotoamatsukami

Names in Uchiha lore are easy to mix up, particularly when short videos list techniques without context. Izanami and Izanagi are related forbidden ocular techniques, but they do not serve the same purpose. Izanagi alters the user's relationship to an unfavorable reality for a brief period; Izanami creates a looping confrontation with the target's choices. Both have grave eye-related costs. An article that treats them as interchangeable will make the Kabuto encounter difficult to understand.

Kotoamatsukami is associated with Shisui Uchiha, not Itachi's original pair of Mangekyō abilities. Itachi later possesses Shisui's eye and arranges a crow-based contingency that uses the technique. That distinction matters because the crow's intervention in the war is a planned safeguard, not evidence that Itachi was born with every famous Uchiha eye power. The Naruto official Shisui birthday column is an especially useful reference for tracing that chain of custody.
Why doesn't Itachi use his strongest attack constantly?

The short answer is that a shinobi is not a menu of infinite resources. Genjutsu can be situational, Mangekyō techniques carry physical cost, some abilities require careful timing and Itachi's illness limits his stamina. His actual decisions reflect goals more complicated than defeating the nearest enemy as quickly as possible. During the Sasuke fight he wants a particular resolution, and in the war he must undo a controlling technique rather than simply inflict more damage.

There is also the narrative issue of information. Itachi often wins space by making another character misunderstand the battlefield. Displaying an advanced technique immediately can reveal his options, leaving fewer surprises. Not every scene can be extrapolated into a ranking of unrelated characters because Naruto's battles reward particular matchups. A specialist in sealing, perception or domain-like containment can trouble a physically stronger opponent. Itachi is dangerous precisely because he knows those distinctions.
Power comparisons that are meaningful—and ones that aren't

Itachi versus Sasuke can be discussed using their actual duel, but not as a clean test between healthy versions with identical motives. Itachi versus Kakashi has direct early-series evidence about genjutsu and timing. Itachi versus Kabuto can be evaluated through the war-arc events and Izanami. By contrast, Itachi versus a character he never fought is a hypothetical. The story may offer clues, but no official scoreboard resolves how its unseen matchups would play out.

A more useful reader checklist asks which version of Itachi is being compared, whether eye contact is possible, whether Susanoo can be maintained, how an opponent deals with illusion, and what goal each fighter pursues. This turns an endless argument into an intelligible analysis. The conclusion can still be uncertain. A strong piece of fandom writing should feel comfortable saying 'the series does not show that' rather than pretending it witnessed a battle that the creators never depicted.
Frequently asked questions

Is Tsukuyomi the same as Kotoamatsukami? No. Tsukuyomi is Itachi's own terrifying time-distorting genjutsu; Kotoamatsukami originated with Shisui's eye. Is Susanoo his strongest move? It may be his most dramatic combined offense and defense, while Izanami has a uniquely consequential result in a specific encounter. There is no official single-number ranking of these techniques. Does Itachi have an Eternal Mangekyō Sharingan? No, his normal Mangekyō powers are not presented as an Eternal Mangekyō upgrade.

Why did his eyes worsen? Repeated use of powerful Mangekyō techniques has serious costs, compounded by his underlying illness. Did the Totsuka Blade seal Orochimaru? The brothers' confrontation shows Itachi using that Susanoo-associated weapon against Orochimaru's manifestation. Can Itachi defeat every shinobi with one glance? The franchise does not support that universal claim. For original context, begin with the official Naruto retrospectives of his battles and the Fourth Ninja War rather than isolated clips.
